## ARGUMENT

### The Court May Consider Documents Incorporated by Reference in the Complaint Without Converting Defendant's Motion into One for Summary Judgment.

Rule 12(d) requires conversion to summary judgment only when "matters outside the pleadings are presented to and not excluded by the court." Fed. R. Civ. P. 12(d). The Ninth Circuit has long held that documents incorporated by reference in a complaint are not "outside the pleadings." A court "may . . . consider certain materials—documents attached to the complaint, documents incorporated by reference in the complaint, or matters of judicial notice—without converting the motion to dismiss into a motion for summary judgment." *United States v. Ritchie*, 342 F.3d 903, 908 (9th Cir. 2003).

**A. The doctrine is well settled in this Circuit.**

The doctrine reaches back at least to *Branch v. Tunnell*, 14 F.3d 449, 454 (9th Cir. 1994), *overruled on other grounds by Galbraith v. County of Santa Clara*, 307 F.3d 1119 (9th Cir. 2002). There, the court held that documents whose contents are alleged in a complaint, and whose authenticity no party questions, may be considered on a Rule 12(b)(6) motion even though they are not physically attached to the pleading. *Id.*; *accord Parrino v. FHP, Inc.*, 146 F.3d 699, 706 (9th Cir. 1998), *superseded by statute on other grounds as stated in Abrego Abrego v. Dow Chem. Co.*, 443 F.3d 676, 681–82 (9th Cir. 2006). The Ninth Circuit has since extended the doctrine to documents on which the plaintiff's claim depends, even if the complaint does not expressly quote them, so long as the defendant submits the document and no party questions its authenticity. *Knievel v. ESPN*, 393 F.3d 1068, 1076 (9th Cir. 2005); *Marder v. Lopez*, 450 F.3d 445, 448 (9th Cir. 2006). The court has applied the doctrine to securities filings and similar public disclosures that form the basis of a plaintiff's allegations. *See In re Silicon Graphics Inc. Sec. Litig.*, 183 F.3d 970, 986 (9th Cir. 1999), *superseded by statute on other grounds as recognized in S. Ferry LP, No. 2 v. Killinger*, 542 F.3d 776, 784 (9th Cir. 2008).

**B. The doctrine rests on sound principles.**

Incorporation by reference "treats certain documents as though they are part of the complaint itself." *Khoja v. Orexigen Therapeutics, Inc.*, 899 F.3d 988, 1002 (9th Cir. 2018). It also "prevents plaintiffs from selecting only portions of documents that support their claims, while omitting portions of those very documents that weaken—or doom—their claims." *Id.* Without it, a plaintiff could defeat a motion to dismiss by quoting a document selectively or by referring to it indirectly while leaving its full text out of the pleading. *See Knievel*, 393 F.3d at 1076. Because the document is treated as part of the complaint, considering it does not convert the motion. *Ritchie*, 342 F.3d at 908.

**C. The doctrine applies here.**

A document is incorporated by reference where the complaint "refers extensively to the document or the document forms the basis of the plaintiff's claim." *Id.* at 907–08; *see also Khoja*, 899 F.3d at 1002. The [DOCUMENT] satisfies this standard. Plaintiff's complaint expressly refers to it at [¶¶ __], and Plaintiff's [claim] depends on its terms and effect. [Describe how the claim rests on the document.] Plaintiff cannot rely on the document to state a claim while asking the Court to ignore the rest of its text. *See Khoja*, 899 F.3d at 1002.

Nor is there any dispute about authenticity. Defendant has submitted a true and complete copy of the document, [Ex. __, Decl. of __ ¶ __], and Plaintiff has no basis to question it, since the complaint itself describes and relies on the document. *See Marder*, 450 F.3d at 448; *Knievel*, 393 F.3d at 1076.

**D. Considering the document does not require the Court to resolve factual disputes.**

Defendant recognizes the limits the Ninth Circuit has placed on the doctrine. A court may not use an incorporated document to resolve factual disputes against a plaintiff, and it may not assume the truth of an incorporated document where doing so would only dispute well-pleaded facts. *Khoja*, 899 F.3d at 1003. Defendant asks for neither. Defendant relies on the document for what it says, which is its plain text, and not for the truth of any disputed matter outside it. The document bears on whether the complaint's allegations about it are plausible. *See id.* at 1002–03; *Ritchie*, 342 F.3d at 908. Defendant does not offer it to create a competing factual narrative.

The Court therefore may, and should, consider the [DOCUMENT] in ruling on this motion under Rule 12(b)(6), without converting the motion into one for summary judgment. *Ritchie*, 342 F.3d at 908.
